Reductive amination is a chemical reaction in organic chemistry where an amine group (NH2) is added to an aldehyde or ketone, reducing the aldehyde or ketone to a primary alcohol in the process. This reaction is often used in organic synthesis to introduce an amine group into a molecule.

The general reaction can be represented as follows:

\[ \text{R-C(=O)-H} + \text{R'-NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{R-C(=O)-NH}_2 + \text{R'-OH} \]

In this reaction, the aldehyde or ketone (R-C(=O)-H) is reduced to a primary alcohol (R-C(=O)-NH2), and the amine (R'-NH2) is formed. The reduction of the carbonyl group (C=O) to a primary alcohol (C-OH) is achieved by the use of a reducing agent, typically a reducing agent like sodium borohydride (NaBH4) or lithium aluminum hydride (LiAlH4).

This reaction is particularly useful in the synthesis of amines and is a key step in the preparation of various organic compounds, including pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals.
